question: Protecting the future of our livestock farms also means protecting consumer health and animal welfare. This implies reducing the harmful effects of factory farming, such as pollution from livestock effluents, the development of antibiotic resistance, the use of growth hormones and other products prohibited by the EU on fodder crops (atrazine), and the import of palm oil cake or maize derived from deforestation.

However, our producers must be able to compete on an equal footing with their competitors from nonEU countries, in particular via the inclusion of mirror clauses in free trade agreements. These clauses would make it possible to impose the same environmental and health standards on all livestock products imported from non-EU countries.

This is the only way to stop the practice of dumping with regard to animal products in international trade. According to some sources, the Commission could launch a public consultation on the post-2027 CAP in the first half of 2024 and DG Agriculture has already led preliminary technical exchanges with relevant parties and the Member States.
Will the Commission, in its preliminary consultations on the post-2027 CAP, support making all imports of agricultural products, particularly meat products, subject to mirror clauses?
answer: On 25 January 2024 President von der Leyen has launched the Strategic dialogue on the future of EU agriculture, with the aim to strengthening the understanding of current and expected challenges, bringing together farmers and other stakeholders from across the agri-food chain.

In this dialogue, different questions will be addressed, such as how to support agriculture within the boundaries of our planet, how to make better use of knowledge and technological innovation, and how to ensure a better perspective to our farmers and rural communities in a competitive world.

The outcome of this dialogue, expected to be concluded during the course of summer 2024, as well as other consultations and exchanges with citizens, stakeholders, Member States and other European institutions, will contribute to the preparation of policy initiatives of the next College of Commissioners, including the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy.
At this stage, it is too early to anticipate the content of such proposals.
